newsitem.title: CHILE: Codelco, Merrill reach agreement on futures deal.
newsitem.headline: Codelco, Merrill reach agreement on futures deal.

text.p: Chilean state copper company Codelco said that Merrill Lynch and Co Inc has agreed to pay it $25 million to end a dispute over failed futures deals.

"Although Merrill Lynch denies having committed any incorrect actions, it will pay Codelco $25 million to put an end to this dispute and avoid the costs that are involved in continuing," said Codelco chief executive Marcos Lima, who read a joint statement from both companies.
He spoke to reporters at the office of the State Defense Council, which has been investigating the deals.
The statement said Codelco did not find evidence of the alleged payment of secret commissions by Merrill to Codelco's former trader Juan Pablo Dvila, who carried out the loss-making futures deals.
Dvila's speculative futures deals cost Codelco around $170 million in 1993 in a financial scandal that shook international copper markets.
Merrill's payment will include $22 million to cover Codelco's losses and $3 million towards its legal costs.
The two companies entered into negotiations to reach a settlement in December 1995 after Codelco told Merrill that it planned to initiate legal action against the brokerage.
The claim was based on charges that "ex-employees of Merrill Lynch by action or ommission facilitated Juan Pablo Dvila's unauthorized speculative operations," said the statement.
"We believed we had a very strong claim against Merrill Lynch and we communicated that to Merrill Lynch very firmly," Codelco's U.S. lawyer Philip Forlenza told the news conference.
"We explained that if this matter was not settled we would file the claim."
One factor persuading Codelco to settle was that under the contract with Merrill all commercial disputes must be settled by arbitration and not in the courts, he said.
"Arbitrators will very quickly make a compromise judgement and so it is very rare to recover all the losses you claim you have suffered," said Forlenza.
Under the terms of the deal, Merrill gave Codelco access to tape recordings, documents and personnel to check the broker's assertion that it had not made any payments to Dvila.

Codelco, the world's largest copper producer, has issued writs in London against Belgian traders Sogemin and Germany's Metallgesellschaft and its trader Wolfgang Becker. Both companies have denied any wrongdoing.
Becker worked for Metallgesellschaft while Dvila was trading with the firm and later moved to run Merrill Lynch's Hamburg office.
Dvila, who was fired when the losses were uncovered in 1994, has been charged with fraud and carrying out business "incompatible" with his position at Codelco.
He was recently released from preventive detention in a Santiago jail to undergo cancer treatment.
